prompt.en: A balanced-output tuner is replaced by one with only an unbalanced output. The window line and dipole are unchanged. Which new boundary needs attention?

text.en: The coax-to-tuner input, because the tuner's matching network balances the line on its output side.

feedback.en: A matching network can transform impedance without providing a balanced output. The replacement's unbalanced output still meets the balanced window line at its output connector.

text.en: The dipole feed point, because the window line carries the tuner's unbalanced current up to the antenna.

feedback.en: Window line is balanced. The balance transition needs attention before that run, not after it.

text.en: The new tuner output feeding the existing balanced line.

feedback.en: The replacement creates an unbalanced-to-balanced transition before the window line begins.

text.en: The midpoint of the window line, to equalize losses in its two halves.

feedback.en: Equal cable halves do not define a balance transition. Follow the electrical boundary instead.

explanation.en: A replacement component can create a new interface requirement even if the antenna itself stays unchanged.

prompt.en: A coax jumper will be wound tightly on a ferrite toroid for common-mode control. Which dielectric choice follows the construction guidance?

text.en: Choose foam because its lower loss also makes it more resistant to compression during winding.

feedback.en: Lower dielectric loss does not mean better resistance to compression. Solid dielectric better supports the centre conductor during tight winding.

text.en: Prefer solid dielectric to help keep the centre conductor from shifting toward the shield.

feedback.en: Solid dielectric supports the conductor during tight winding, reducing the risk of a short.

text.en: Choose the thinnest insulation because the shield alone keeps the conductor centred.

feedback.en: The dielectric separates and supports the conductors. Thinner insulation is not automatically safer.

text.en: Treat foam and solid dielectric as mechanically identical if both cables have the same Z0.

feedback.en: Equal characteristic impedance does not establish identical mechanical behaviour under tight winding.

explanation.en: Choose cable for its mechanical job as well as attenuation and characteristic impedance.

prompt.en: An older coax jumper passes a low-current continuity check. During a brief transmit test its connector becomes warm and RF readings turn intermittent. Which explanation best fits both observations?

text.en: The continuity pass rules out a resistive contact; reflections from the antenna explain the heating instead.

feedback.en: A contact can pass a small test current yet heat under load. The continuity result does not rule out contact resistance, and reflections do not explain away the intermittent connector symptom.

text.en: The heating is ordinary distributed cable loss, with the connector simply showing the temperature change first.

feedback.en: Ordinary distributed loss does not explain intermittent behaviour at a warming connector. The local symptom points to the connection rather than normal attenuation along the cable.

text.en: The cable's nominal impedance rises as it warms, so intermittent RF readings are expected from an intact connector.

feedback.en: Normal warming does not make an intact connector intermittent. A cable's nominal impedance is not an explanation for this localized heating and loss of reliable contact.

text.en: A resistive contact can pass the small test current yet heat and become intermittent under transmit load.

feedback.en: The test current can pass through a poor contact. Greater current produces more heating at that resistance; inspect and restore or replace the faulty connection before reuse.

explanation.en: A low-current continuity pass can coexist with a contact fault under transmit load. Localized heating and intermittent readings are different evidence from an unbroken path at small current.
